True.
At the end of the First World War all the nations felt that such a war should not happen again and that some measures needed to be taken to achieve that end. An international organisation called the League of Nations was established out of this thinking. It became an important platform to solve international disputes and carry out negotiations, and its main responsibility was understood to be to avoid war.

False.
During the Cold War most countries of the world joined either of the two super power blocs, and such a division of the nations of the world into two groups is called bipolarisation. So the Cold War made the world bipolar, not unipolar. A unipolar system is one in which there is only one super power and several countries are dependent upon it. That situation came about only after the Cold War ended and the Soviet Russia disintegrated, when America remained the only super power in world politics.

True.
The then President of the Soviet Russia, Mikhail Gorbachev, implemented the policies of Perestroika (Restructuring) and Glasnost (Openness). Due to these policies the control over the media was reduced and important changes took place in the political and economic spheres, that is, these spheres were restructured. The chapter says that this gave impetus to democracy. The East European countries under the influence of the Soviet Russia also adopted the capitalist and democratic paths and the regimes there changed.

The concept of Cold War is used to describe the condition where there is no actual war, but there are such tensions in the circumstances that they may be responsible to cause war. America and the Soviet Russia, who were allies in the Second World War, became competitors as soon as the war got over, and their cooperation gave way to rivalry. This rivalry occupied about 40 to 45 years of international politics, from 1945 to 1991. There was no open war between the two countries, but the struggle for power, the arms race, the differences in ideologies and the attitude of checkmating each other by strategies and counter-strategies kept their relations so tense that it seemed a war would erupt any time.

In the period of the Cold War, while the world was becoming bipolar, there were some countries which did not want to join the super power rivalry. Such nations decided to stay out of the cold war rivalry, and their policy is known as non-alignment. It was an important movement during the Cold War, supported by the Asian and African countries which became independent after the Second World War. The movement started from 1961 under the leadership of India's Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, President of Yugoslavia Marshall Tito, President of Egypt Gamal Abdal Nasser, President of Indonesia Dr Sukarno and President of Ghana Dr Kwame Nkrumah. It opposed colonialism, imperialism and racism, and encouraged the resolution of international disputes by peaceful means.

All the countries of the world are dependent on each other for one reason or the other. However big, prosperous or developed a nation may be, it can never be self-sufficient about all its needs. Even big nations have to depend upon other big and small nations. This mutual dependence of nations upon one another is called interdependence, and it is an important feature of the international system, that is, of today's global system.

During the Cold War, most countries of the world joined either of the two super power blocs. Such a division of the nations of the world in two groups is called bipolarisation. Both the super powers made efforts to pull smaller countries into their respective blocs, and as a result Europe was ideologically divided: the Western European countries joined the bloc led by America, while the Eastern European countries joined the bloc led by the Soviet Russia. Because of this division the scope of the Cold War increased and the sphere of tension spread.

After the end of the Cold War, trade and economic relations between countries became more open. Capital, labour, markets and information began circulating globally and the give and take of ideas among people all over the world grew. Due to the revolution in information technology, different events and developments began to be known everywhere, and the boundaries between nations did not remain as sacrosanct as they were before. All these processes together are called globalisation. Globalisation has brought benefits, but it has also caused losses; for example, trade increased and plenty of products became available in the markets, but the gap between the poor and the rich nations did not reduce.

Political - earlier empires in Europe collapsed and new nations came into being; movements for independence started in the colonies in Africa and Asia and challenged the hegemony of the European nations; autocratic regimes came up in Germany, Italy, Spain and other countries. | Economic - it proved far more destructive and more widespread than the First World War and more advanced technology was employed in it; the countries which took part once again faced a situation of economic crisis. Political - America dropped two nuclear weapons on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6th and 9th August 1945; the war ended with the defeat of Germany in Europe and of Japan in Asia; the Cold War between America and the Soviet Russia began; the Asian and African countries became independent after this war. |
| 4. International Organisations established after the War | The League of Nations was established, out of the feeling that such a war should not happen again. It became an important platform to solve international disputes and carry out negotiations, and its main responsibility was understood to be to avoid war. [Note: the chapter does not state which international organisation was established after the Second World War. It names the United Nations elsewhere, but only to say that the responsibility of the United Nations increased after the Cold War; it nowhere says when the United Nations was established.]

The Cold War had dominated international politics since 1945, and it came to an end towards the end of the last century. The chapter gives the following reasons for it. (1) The Soviet Russia adopted the policy of opening up the economy and the State loosened up its control of the economy. (2) The then President of the Soviet Russia, Mikhail Gorbachev, implemented the policies of Perestroika (Restructuring) and Glasnost (Openness); due to these the control over the media reduced, the political and economic spheres were restructured, and this gave impetus to democracy. (3) The East European countries under the influence of the Soviet Russia adopted the capitalist and democratic paths, and the regimes there changed. (4) The Soviet Russia disintegrated and several new nations were created out of it, Russia being the biggest country in the former Soviet Russia.

The Cold War came to an end with the disintegration of the Soviet Russia, which till then had been a super power, and major changes took place in world politics. America remained the only super power in world politics. A conducive atmosphere prevailed for the growth in trade and economic relations between and among nations, and capital, labour, market and information circulated throughout the world, while ideas too spread freely. As all nations decided to give priority to trade relations, the idea of giving aid to other nations fell behind and efforts began to be made to establish economic relations instead; the description of a country which was opposed to another changed from enemy nation to rival nation. The responsibility of the United Nations increased, as it now had to take more concrete steps to maintain global peace and security. Environmental protection, fostering of human rights, gender equality and management of natural calamities now acquired a global dimension.
